newsitem.title: CHINA: China July M1 rises 15 percent, M2 27 percent.
newsitem.headline: China July M1 rises 15 percent, M2 27 percent.

text.p: China's M1 measure of money supply rose in July by 15 percent over a year earlier and M2 by 27 percent, the official China Securities newspaper said on Saturday, quoting central bank governor Dai Xianglong.
He said that the debt-equity ratio of China's 1,200 big state firms fell to 59 percent by the end of June.

He said the growth in M1 and M2 in July was sharply lower than in previous years. Monetary supply must be appropriate, with growth in M1 substantially higher than the rise in prices and economic growth, Dai said.
Macro-control of the economy must increasily rely on interest rates and other economic levers and indirect means, he said.
Dai said the problems of state firms were not due to a shortage of money.
In the first half of 1996, bank deposits by state firms rose 26 percent over the same 1995 period and loans by state banks increased by 100 billion yuan over the year earlier, he said.
Resolving the problem of state firms depended on speeding up reforms, changing their economic structure, developing the domestic and foreign markets and finding new sources of growth, Dai said.
He said China was making great progress in developing its financial markets, with state commercial banks as their base as well as a wide range of other financial institutions.
China had set up a national interbank market and had more than 400 companies listed on its stock exchanges, with stock turnover in the first seven months of the year of 630 billion yuan, he said.
